chapter_theme: A ruler's power depends on those greater than himself whom he can win and keep, and above all on those who will correct him. The chapter counts this as the highest strength and calls its lack self-destruction.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: who the great are and how to win them (441-442), the distinction of having them (443-445), the fruits (446-447), and the fault of lacking them (448-450).

441.reading: Knowing their worth and the way to go about it, choose the friendship of those of understanding who have matured in knowledge of virtue.
441.nuance: மூத்த is not simply age: Parimelazhagar counts maturity in understanding, character and years. The verse doesn't say what office such people hold, though Manakkudavar takes them to be priests. For Parimelazhagar திறன் is the way of winning them, and for Manakkudavar it is their capacities.

442.reading: Cherish and take as support those who have the quality of removing the affliction that has come and guarding before against what has not.

positions.position: These are priests and ministers: priests handle afflictions from the gods by rites, and ministers those from people by the four policies.
These are ministers. He takes the verse's general word to refer to them, leaving priests to 441.

443.reading: To cherish the great and make them one's own is the rarest of all rare things.
443.nuance: அரிது can mean hard to do, as Manakkudavar has it, or rare to attain, as Parimelazhagar does. The second adds his observation that a king who can have every rare thing still prizes this one, because the others come through it.

444.reading: To conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own is the chief of all strengths.
444.nuance: A paradox of power: the supreme strength is standing under someone. Parimelazhagar's தாம் அவர் வழிநின்று makes the king the follower, and he ranks this above wealth, army and fortress on the ground that it reaches afflictions they can't.

445.reading: Since counsellors serve as his eyes, a ruler must take his counsellors after counsel.
445.nuance: The verse plays on சூழ், which means to deliberate, to plot and to surround, and the commentators split along those senses.

positions.position: The king should examine his counsellors before taking them on, because they are his eyes.
positions.quote: அரசன் அத்தன்மையராய அமைச்சரை ஆராய்ந்து தனக்குத் துணையாகக் கொள்க.

positions.position: The king should be able to outplot and kill those who plot to kill him.
positions.quote: அரசன் தன்னைச் சூழ்ச்சியாற் கொல்ல நினைப்பாரைத் தானுஞ் சூழ்ச்சியாற் கொல்லவல்லவனாதல்

positions.position: The ruler benefits by keeping the wise around him.

446.reading: There is nothing enemies can do against one able to carry himself as one of the company of the worthy.
446.nuance: தான் ஒழுக வல்லான்: having good company isn't enough; he too must act accordingly. It is the ability that protects, not only the associates.

447.reading: Who has the standing to ruin those who keep as their support people who will rebuke them?
447.nuance: ஆள்வாரை: such people must actually be employed and valued. Parimelazhagar adds that the rebuker needs to be free of the same faults and to love the king, so rebuke alone doesn't qualify.

448.reading: A ruler without the guard of those who rebuke will perish even with no one to ruin him.
448.nuance: Parimelazhagar's image is an elephant with no mahout, going off the path and ruining itself. கெடுப்பார் இலானும் makes enemies unnecessary to the story, and 447 and 448 form a pair, protection and exposure.

449.reading: Those without capital have no profit; those without the support of a pillar have no standing.
449.nuance: A merchant's image for a king's court. Allies are the principal rather than the return: everything else is earned on them. The verse doesn't limit itself to kings; the older commentators supply that.

450.reading: To let go one's tie with the good is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many.
450.nuance: Pope and Kalaignar read கைவிடல் as abandoning a tie, whereas Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it as failing to take the great as support. His reason is practical: there are ways out of many enemies, but none out of having no good company.

links.note: 444 ranks support as the chief of strengths. 471 lists it as one of four to weigh before acting, alongside the task and the opponent. The superlative here gets absorbed into a calculation there.

434 calls one's own fault the only enemy that brings ruin. 448 shows the mechanism: without those who rebuke, no outside enemy is needed. Self-correction turns out to be something a person needs other people for.
